title: What is Apache Flink — another engine for processing data, but designed specially for real-time streaming (processes each event as it arrives, not in batches like Spark's default mode).

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Apache Flink is an open-source distributed stream-processing engine built for true record-at-a-time processing with very low latency and strong correctness guarantees. Unlike micro-batch systems, Flink treats a stream as the fundamental primitive and processes each event as it arrives. It provides event-time processing with watermarks, rich keyed and windowed state managed in state backends, and exactly-once semantics via distributed checkpointing. Flink treats batch as a special, bounded case of streaming.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the National Bank of India's fraud desk. Spark's default mode is like a supervisor who collects card swipes into small stacks and checks each stack every few seconds. Flink is like a sharp officer who inspects every single swipe the instant it lands on the counter, remembers each customer's recent pattern in their head (state), and can tell that Priya's card was used in two cities one minute apart — right now, not a few seconds late. Flink also keeps a reliable notebook (checkpoint) so if the officer faints, a replacement resumes from the exact last page with no swipe double-counted.

**One line to remember:** Flink is a true event-at-a-time streaming engine with event-time windows, keyed state, and exactly-once guarantees for real-time processing.

sections.s2_technical:
Flink's core model is the dataflow: your program is a graph of operators (sources, transformations, sinks) through which events flow continuously. Every event is processed as it arrives, so latency can be in the low milliseconds, whereas Spark Structured Streaming's default micro-batch groups events and carries a small latency floor. This record-at-a-time design is Flink's signature difference.

Flink's handling of time is a standout feature. It distinguishes event-time (when the event actually happened, carried in the record) from processing-time (when the engine sees it). Because events arrive late and out of order in the real world, Flink uses watermarks, which are markers that flow with the stream saying "I believe I have seen all events up to time T". A window like "count card swipes per account per minute" fires based on event-time and watermarks, with configurable allowed lateness for stragglers. You express this as a keyed, windowed aggregation: `stream.keyBy(Txn::getAccountId).window(TumblingEventTimeWindows.of(Time.minutes(1))).sum("amount")`, which groups by account and sums per one-minute window.

State is first-class in Flink. Operators can keep keyed state — for example, each account's running count or last-seen location — and Flink manages that state in a state backend, which can be in memory or on disk (RocksDB) for very large state. This makes stateful stream processing, like running fraud rules that depend on history, natural and scalable.

Correctness is guaranteed by distributed checkpointing. Flink periodically takes a consistent snapshot of all operator state and source offsets using a lightweight barrier algorithm. If a node fails, Flink restores the latest checkpoint and replays from the saved offsets, giving exactly-once state semantics; combined with transactional sinks it extends to exactly-once end-to-end. A senior nuance is that Flink unifies batch and streaming by treating a bounded dataset as a finite stream, so the same API serves both. For a bank, Flink is the engine of choice when you need real-time fraud scoring, live risk limits, or instant settlement signals where every millisecond and every guarantee matters.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India must react to each card swipe the instant it happens, not a few seconds later in a batch. This is exactly Flink's record-at-a-time processing — handle every event on arrival.

Problem 2 — Fraud rules depend on recent history, like how many high-value swipes an account made in the last minute. This is exactly keyed state plus a time window — Flink keeps per-account state and aggregates over a window.

Problem 3 — If the engine crashes, we must resume exactly where we left off without double-counting. This is exactly checkpointing — snapshot state and offsets, restore on failure.

Because running a real Flink cluster is heavy, the mini-project faithfully simulates Flink's model in plain Java. `Event` carries an account id, amount, and event-time. `FlinkStyleProcessor` processes events one at a time (`processElement`), maintains keyed per-account windowed state, fires a fraud alert when a one-minute window exceeds a count threshold, and supports `checkpoint()` and `restore()` to prove fault tolerance. The demo streams several swipes for Rajesh and Priya and shows a per-account windowed alert firing in real time.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a stream of five card-swipe events within a 30-second span, four of them belonging to Rajesh (SAV2001), against a rule of at most three swipes per one-minute window.

Step 1 — First event arrives. Rajesh's 1200 swipe is processed the instant it arrives. The processor creates keyed state for SAV2001 with a window starting at the event time and a count of one.

Step 2 — Second event. Priya's 5000 swipe arrives five seconds later. It gets its own keyed state under CUR3001, independent of Rajesh. Each key has its own window.

Step 3 — Third event and checkpoint. Rajesh's second swipe (900) arrives; his window count becomes two. Right after this, the demo takes a checkpoint, snapshotting the keyed state, then simulates a crash and restores from that snapshot, proving state survives failure.

Step 4 — Fourth event. Rajesh's third swipe (700) arrives; his count becomes three, still at the limit, so no alert yet.

Step 5 — Fifth event triggers alert. Rajesh's fourth swipe (600) arrives within the same one-minute window; his count becomes four, exceeding the limit of three, so a fraud alert fires immediately in real time. The whole decision happened event-by-event with per-account state that survived a checkpoint and restore.

```
INFO: EVENT SAV2001 amt=1200 windowCount=1
INFO: EVENT CUR3001 amt=5000 windowCount=1
INFO: EVENT SAV2001 amt=900 windowCount=2
INFO: CHECKPOINT: snapshotting keyed state
WARNING: RESTORED keyed state from checkpoint
INFO: EVENT SAV2001 amt=700 windowCount=3
INFO: EVENT SAV2001 amt=600 windowCount=4
SEVERE: FRAUD ALERT: SAV2001 exceeded 3 swipes within 60s
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Apache Flink is an open-source distributed stream-processing engine built for true record-at-a-time processing with very low latency and strong correctness guarantees. Its signature difference from a micro-batch system like Spark Structured Streaming is that Flink treats a stream as the fundamental primitive and processes each event the instant it arrives, rather than grouping events into small batches, so latency can be in the low milliseconds. Flink even treats batch as a special case of streaming over a bounded dataset, so one API serves both.

Flink's standout features are time handling, state, and correctness. For time, it distinguishes event-time, when the event actually happened, from processing-time, when the engine sees it, and because real-world events arrive late and out of order, it uses watermarks to decide when a window is complete, with configurable allowed lateness. For state, keyed state is first-class: each key, such as an account, can keep running state like a count or last-seen location, managed in a state backend that can be in memory or RocksDB for very large state, which makes stateful fraud rules natural and scalable. For correctness, Flink takes periodic distributed checkpoints of all operator state and source offsets using lightweight barriers, so after a failure it restores the latest checkpoint and replays from saved offsets, giving exactly-once state semantics, and with transactional sinks that extends to exactly-once end to end.

In my project at the National Bank of India this was the engine we reached for whenever real time and correctness both mattered, like real-time fraud scoring. Conceptually the job keyed the swipe stream by account, kept a per-account count inside a one-minute event-time window, and fired an alert the instant an account exceeded its allowed swipes, and because state was checkpointed, even a mid-stream crash and restore did not lose the running counts or double-count a swipe. That combination of event-at-a-time latency, rich keyed state, event-time windows, and exactly-once guarantees is exactly why a bank chooses Flink for its most demanding streaming workloads.

keyPoints: Apache Flink: true event-time stream processing
Record-at-a-time: lower latency than Spark micro-batch
Event time vs processing time: correct results despite delays
State management: RocksDB backend for large state
